entries.text: At Hearth, the two pause as Wren spots a familiar object lying near the path. "That's the purse from the festival shopper, isn't it? Let's see what the list says — maybe we can find the owner before they worry too much." Ash stoops, picks the purse up, and opens it to study the shopping list tucked inside, reading the owner's details. "Aye, the frayed cord's a fair mark. Let's walk it to the Market and see who claims it. Honest work, that," Wren suggests they return the purse to the Market owner, noting that because the cord is frayed, the owner will be able to tell the purse is truly theirs.

entries.text: At Hearth, Wren moves toward the Market, while Ash lingers, observing the surroundings. "Ash, while you're looking around — let's peek at that shopping list together. Maybe the owner's name is on it, so we don't have to wait for them to come to us."

entries.title: The Market stalls hummed with the midday crowd, and Hearth's familiar scents of bread and salt hung in the air.
entries.text: The Market stalls hummed with the midday crowd, and Hearth's familiar scents of bread and salt hung in the air. Ash left the common room behind and made his way into the Market, his steps deliberate. Wren called out across the stalls, asking if anyone had dropped a purse with a frayed cord and a shopping list, then watched for an owner to respond. The call worked — a hopeful, patient wait that drew a few curious glances.

entries.text: The scene takes place at the Market, where the morning crowd shuffles between stalls and the air carries the smell of fresh produce. Wren turns to Ash, gesturing at a crumpled shopping list in her hand, trying to communicate the idea that they should read it together to find the owner's name. Ash studies the list closely, taking in the handwriting and the smudges of ink, observing every detail for a clue. "Good thinking. Let's open it up and see who we're hunting for."

entries.text: At the bustling Market, an effort to get the shopping list read aloud stirred between two people, each hoping to learn the owner's name.

entries.text: The two of them stand amid the bustle of the Market, the morning light catching the stalls and the crowd moving between them. Ash tries to share what they've found with Wren, explaining that the list has no name but mentions flour for the festival bread, which points to the baker's stall. Wren, in turn, asks Ash whether the list carried any name or clue at all. "No name yet, Wren — just a list of goods. But the handwriting's neat, and there's a smudge of red clay on the corner. That's the kind of clay they use for the potter's stall at the far end. Let's ask there." "No name — but flour for festival bread is a strong clue. Let's go ask at the baker's stall together." With that, the two turn and head through the Market toward the baker's stall, the list still in hand.

entries.title: The market hums with festival bustle as Marta the festival baker stands among her stalls, eyeing the trio before her.
entries.text: The market hums with festival bustle as Marta the festival baker stands among her stalls, eyeing the trio before her. Marta, the list calls for festival flour — has it reached your stall yet? If so, that might be your flour and the purse's owner nearby. Marta, Ash is asking you about that shopping list — the one with the flour for the festival bread. Do you know whose handwriting that is? We're hoping to return the purse to its owner. That list you're asking about — I recognize the stitching on the purse it came from. It belongs to Dryden, the miller's son. He orders my flour every festival. If you help find my missing flour, I'll tell you where to find him. Ash attempts to ask Marta about the shopping list and its owner, pressing on the purse's frayed cord to see if it matches her customers or her own. We're on the trail of that purse's owner — the list says flour for the festival bread. If that's your flour, maybe you know who was shopping for you? I see the question shift to Wren, and Marta turns to her with a knowing look. That purse—I know the stitching. It belongs to old Bessie from the mill; she always carries that frayed cord. She's a customer of mine.

entries.title: Wren tries to speak with Marta the festival baker about: Dryden the miller's son and helping find the missing flour
entries.text: Wren tries to speak with Marta the festival baker about: Dryden the miller's son and helping find the missing flour Ash tries to speak with Marta the festival baker about: Offer to help find the missing flour in exchange for Dryden's location Marta the festival baker tries to speak with Ash about: Confirm the deal: help find flour, I'll tell where Dryden is If you truly can find my missing flour, I'll tell you where Dryden is. But be quick—the festival bread won't wait. Ash, that's a good plan—finding the flour might also lead us to the purse's owner. Let's both help Marta. Ash, Marta's offering a trade — help her track down the missing flour, and she'll point us to Dryden. I say we take it; finding that flour might also lead us to the purse's owner. Wren, aye—Dryden's the one with the frayed cord. But I can't do much till my flour turns up; the festival loaves won't rise without it. Help me find it and I'll take you straight to him. Dryden, then — the miller's son. Tell me plainly what flour you're missing and where it was meant to go, and I'll help you hunt it down before the festival.

entries.text: At the Market, the three of them trade questions. Wren asks Marta whether the name on the purse means anything, or whether the flour list rings a bell. Marta turns the question back on Ash: the ledger claims her flour was delivered last week—so where has it gone, and what does Ash know about the delivery boy? And Ash wants to know when the flour was last seen, and whether any strangers or deliveries came by before it vanished. Wren turns to Marta: "Marta, if the ledger says the flour was delivered, maybe the delivery boy can tell us where he actually left it. Let's find that boy — he might have dropped it somewhere, or someone else took it before it reached you." Marta the festival baker tells Ash: "It was late yesterday, after the market shut. I set the sacks behind my stall for the night—no strangers about that I saw, but the cord on the last sack was clean-cut, not frayed. That's what troubles me." Ash answers Marta: "A ledger saying the flour was already delivered last week? Then either that delivery boy's crooked, or the ledger's lying. Let's not guess—let's go to the mill and ask Dryden himself to show us the page. The flour had to go somewhere." Wren agrees with Ash: "Ash, I'll back you up on that. Let's also ask Marta if she kept a list of what flour went where—the purse list might match her order." Marta the festival baker says to Wren: "That purse — I've seen its stitching before; it belongs to Dryden's sister, Elara. And the flour list, it's the order I sent to the mill last week — it should've been delivered by now, but the sacks never came."

entries.title: At the market, Ash asks Wren whether they should check Dryden's mill for the ledger proving the flour delivery.
entries.text: At the market, Ash asks Wren whether they should check Dryden's mill for the ledger proving the flour delivery. Pip presses Marta about the ledger showing flour delivered to her last week, while Wren asks if she saw any delivery boy or stranger and whether she knows the purse's owner. Marta tells Ash about the cut cord and where to find the delivery boy. "I was the delivery boy, Wren. I brought the flour to Marta last week—it's all in the ledger. Ask her about the purse, but she'll likely lie." Wren tells Pip the ledger may be wrong or the delivery boy crooked, and suggests pressing Dryden at the mill for the truth—also noting the purse is Elara's and they should ask Dryden about his sister and the flour together. "I'm right here, Marta. You talk about the cut cord and the delivery boy — I've got the ledger, and it shows your name on the flour. So what's this about where I'm meant to be?" "Where is it? I wish I knew. The sacks were behind my stall come nightfall, and by dawn they were gone, the cord clean-cut. That ledger's pure lie—I never signed for a thing." "Ash, yes—let's go to the mill. If the ledger is right, we'll catch the lie; if not, we'll find where the flour truly went. And I'd like to see Dryden's sister Elara while we're there—that purse is hers."

entries.title: At the Market, the group gathers around as the argument over the missing flour and Elara's purse pulls at them from ever
entries.text: At the Market, the group gathers around as the argument over the missing flour and Elara's purse pulls at them from every direction. Wren turns to Marta, pressing for answers before anyone sets off, asking directly about the purse and what they might be walking into at the mill. Wren says to Marta the festival baker: "Marta, if the purse is Elara's, did she buy the flour herself or did she send someone? And what did she want it for—if we're to bring it to the mill, I'd like to know what we're walking into." Pip cuts in, waving the ledger as he insists they settle this together in front of Dryden rather than sending messages. Pip says to Marta the festival baker: "Marta, you're sending Wren off with the purse—but I've got the ledger right here, and it says the flour was delivered to you. Let's get to the mill together and settle this in front of Dryden, not send messages back and forth." Marta's voice sharpens as she challenges Pip's claim directly, demanding to know where the sacks were left and denying she ever signed for them. Marta the festival baker says to Pip: "Pip, you show me that ledger line. I never signed for a thing, and my sacks were gone by dawn with the cord cut clean. If you claim delivery, you tell me where you left them—then we'll see who's lying." Ash looks between them, weighing the ledger's claim against Marta's word, and admits that if the delivery is a lie, he wants to know where those sacks really went.
